extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, policymakers, PTO officials, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality of an issued patent grant by using examiner time, prosecution indicators, and related empirical/administrative markers to infer likely validity and downstream litigation risk; also informing policy reforms to improve ex ante examination. Suitable for policy analysis and patent-quality evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Time as Quality Input
rubrics_metrics.description: An application that received above-median examiner time per claim is more reliably examined; an application that received below-median time should be discounted (likely under-examined). Time per claim is the appropriate unit (since claim complexity drives examination effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use GS-grade time-budget tables to compute time per claim; compare actual time used to allocated time. Treat above-median time per claim as a positive quality signal and below-median as a negative signal when evaluating individual grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal Time → Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Each additional hour of examiner time reduces grant probability of marginal applications by a measurable amount, and the patents not granted on the margin are the ones most likely to be invalidated downstream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret small increases in examiner time as materially reducing the issuance of low-quality patents, especially among marginal applications. Use marginal-time estimates when modeling expected downstream invalidation rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation Concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: A small fraction of granted patents account for most litigation costs; better examination at the margin disproportionately prevents these high-cost downstream cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing social value of examination, weight improvements that prevent patents likely to be involved in concentrated litigation more heavily than average improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB Predictability from Examination Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents that survive thorough examination are less likely to be instituted into IPR; PTAB savings reflect avoided low-quality grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PTAB institution and IPR outcomes as downstream validation of ex ante examination quality; lower institution rates for thoroughly examined patents support quality inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple Substantive Office Actions as Quality Marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple substantive office actions = sustained examiner attention and is a marker of substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count the number of substantive office actions in prosecution. Multiple rounds before allowance indicate deeper examination and higher expected patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner-Driven Prior-Art Search Beyond Applicant IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner cites prior art beyond applicant Information Disclosure Statements (IDS) indicates quality work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the provenance of cited art; examiner-initiated citations signal broader search and stronger examination than reliance solely on applicant-submitted art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive 112 Issues Addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive 112 rejections and their resolution are a marker of thorough review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of meaningful 112 engagement (written-description/enablement) in prosecution suggests careful scrutiny of claim support and scope; absence reduces confidence in quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction Requirement Applied Where Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of restriction requirements where appropriate indicates careful claim-scope management during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate restriction practice as a positive quality indicator — it reflects examiner attention to claim clarity and proper prosecution procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Amendments Narrowing Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner amendments that narrow claims during prosecution are a sign of substantive examination and quality-focused resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify examiner-originated claim narrowings as evidence that examination constrained overbroad claims, improving expected patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-Action Allowance with No Rejections (Weak Marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-action allowance with no rejections is a weak examination marker and may indicate time-constrained or cursory review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat first-action allowances without prior rejections skeptically; they are correlated with lower downstream validity and higher likelihood of being low-quality grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Cited Art Originates from Applicant IDS (Weak Marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: When all cited prior art comes from the applicant's IDS, this indicates limited examiner search and is a weak/negative quality marker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner citations mirror only applicant-supplied art, downgrade confidence in the examination's thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single Short Office Action Followed by Allowance (Weak Marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single short office action followed quickly by allowance is indicative of limited examination and is a weak quality signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, perfunctory office actions followed by allowance should be flagged as potential shortcuts; combine with other indicators before concluding quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Substantive 112 Engagement (Weak Marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of meaningful 112 issues during prosecution suggests lack of substantive review and is a weak quality indicator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence/absence of 112 scrutiny as a binary signal: no engagement lowers expected patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior Examiner with High Allowance Rate (Weak Marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior examiners (higher GS grade) who nonetheless have high allowance rates may be operating under time-compressed conditions and this can be a weak quality signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for grade-level time allocation disparities: high allowance rates by senior examiners may reflect compressed per-case time rather than substantive review; investigate time budgets and case complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Four-Test for Individual Grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Four-part test for judging an issued patent: (1) Was examination conducted under standard time allocation or compressed time? (2) Did the examiner make substantive use of the allocated time (multiple actions, broad search)? (3) Are there indicators of quality-degrading shortcuts (first-action allowance, applicant-only art)? (4) Does the prosecution history reflect the time investment a quality examination requires?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all four tests together; a patent passing all four is reliably examined. Use prosecution history, time-allocation data, and citation provenance to apply each prong. Failures on one or more prongs indicate lower expected quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check whether Examination Used Allocated Time or Was Compressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Was examination conducted under standard time allocation or compressed time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare actual exam time against GS-grade allocated budgets; compressed-time examinations should be treated as higher risk for quality deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for Substantive Use of Allocated Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the examiner make substantive use of the allocated time (e.g., multiple actions, broad search)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of substantive time use includes sustained back-and-forth office actions, examiner-initiated prior art, and thorough 112 engagement; use these as positive signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for Indicators of Quality-Degrading Shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there indicators of shortcuts: first-action allowance, applicant-only cited art, single short office action, no 112 engagement, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate shortcut indicators to form a negative quality score; single indicators raise suspicion but multiple indicators strengthen the inference of low-quality examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution History Reflects Time Investment Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the prosecution history reflect the time investment a quality examination requires?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine length, substance, and content of prosecution documents. Substantive rejections, examiner-cited art beyond IDS, and claim amendments indicate time investment; sparse histories suggest under-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Recommendation: Increase Examiner Time Across the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality grants require more time than current allocation provides; increasing examiner time broadly improves expected social welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frakes & Wasserman's cost–benefit calculation (doubling exam time yields net societal benefit ≈ $244M/year) supports broad time increases, funded appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Recommendation: Decouple Time from GS Promotion / Equalize Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Decouple time allocation from GS promotion so senior examiners handling complex cases are not disadvantaged by lower per-case time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform time budgets across grades to reflect case complexity, preventing under-resourcing of complex prosecutions handled by higher-grade examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Recommendation: Substantive Examination Audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce random substantive audits of issued patents to provide feedback to art units about systemic quality issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audit findings to adjust practices and time allocations; audits should target substantive examination features (search quality, 112 engagement, office-action depth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Recommendation: Examiner Performance Metrics Tied to Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace or supplement production-focused metrics with quality-adjusted metrics that reward substantive examination rather than throughput.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design metrics to capture time used, depth of search, examiner-originated citations, and substantive rejections; avoid incentives that encourage cursory allowances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Recommendation: Higher User Fees to Fund Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise user fees targeted to examination (not maintenance) to fund higher-quality ex ante examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee design should direct revenue to hiring/training and time budgets for examiners to achieve measurable quality gains rather than general PTO budget items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–Benefit Standard for Allocating Examination Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a social-cost-minimizing framework to compare ex ante examination cost against ex post litigation and PTAB costs; Frakes & Wasserman estimate that marginal increases in examiner time can yield net social benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting policy, model marginal examiner-time costs against expected litigation and PTAB savings; prioritize investments where marginal exam time prevents high-cost downstream disputes.
